text:
I watched my agent optimize itself into a polite, useless idiot.
Using an LLM to judge an LLM's prompt evolution is circular logic.
It creates a feedback loop of garbage.
Your system needs an anchor that doesn't hallucinate.
---
LLM-as-a-Judge is a lazy shortcut.
It tells you the prompt "looks better" because the tone changed.
The agent swapped a `filter` for a `map` because the LLM judge thought it "read better".
Your agent gets more polite but less accurate.
You're optimizing for aesthetics while the core logic rots.
---
Vibes don't scale.
I replaced subjective grading with four deterministic anchors.
These don't guess.
They measure the delta between the instruction and the execution reality.
If the pass rate stays at 82%, the prompt dies.
---
First is structural integrity.
The output must match the required schema every single time.
Second is token-to-signal ratio.
Shorter prompts that produce the same result win.
---
Third is redundant loops.
I track the number of redundant steps the agent takes to reach a conclusion.
Fourth is edge case pass rate.
The evolution engine must prove it handled the failures the previous version couldn't.
---
The system generates ten variations per cycle.
It runs them through the automated test suite.
It only keeps the version that beats the baseline on all four metrics.
It's Darwinism for code.
---
Stop trusting models to grade their own homework.
An agent that can't measure itself is just a stochastic parrot on a treadmill.
Engineering is about building systems that fail predictably.
Real progress is measured in bits and schemas, not adjectives.
---
Are you still using vibes to grade your prompts or have you moved to deterministic testing?

#AIEngineering #LLM #PromptEngineering
idea_source: How I built a self-improving AI agent that evolves its own prompts
